newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong welcomes invitation to join BIS.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong welcomes invitation to join BIS.

text.p: Hong Kong has welcomed an invitation to join the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), saying it has boosted the territory's standing prior to its 1997 return to Chinese rule.

"The invitation to join the BIS is a clear recognition of Hong Kong's status as a leading and autonomous international financial centre, and Hong Kong's increasingly active role in cooperation among central banks," Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said in a statement issued late on Monday.

Hong Kong was one of nine countries invited to join the BIS, central bank to the world's central banks, which is enlarging its membership for the first time in 25 years as it seeks to play a more global role.
The BIS said its board of directors would invite the nine central banks to become members by subscribing to BIS shares.

The decision by the BIS was announced at its headquarters in in Basle, Switzerland, on Monday. The new members will not change the decision-making structure of the BIS, which is headed by a board of directors made up of the Group of 10 industrial nations.
The move strengthens the British colony's standing in world financial markets in the lead-up to its reversion to Chinese rule next year.

Its post-handover position has been further affirmed by China's central bank, the People's Bank of China, being asked to participate as a separate member -- recognition that the two financial systems will remain separate after 1997.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, which will represent the territory on the BIS, said the invitation demonstrated the international financial community was fully supportive of the one country, two systems policy enshrined in Hong Kong's post-1997 mini-constitution, the Basic Law.
Beijing has promised Hong Kong "a high degree of autonomy" after Britain hands the colony back to the China at midnight on June 30, next year.
Total membership of the BIS is now 32 central banks, all of which are either European or North American with the exception of Japan, Australia and South Africa.
